Taveta weaver (Ploceus castaneiceps) is a highly social ploceid species inhabiting the savanna woodlands and papyrus swamps of East Africa. Incubation experiments conducted at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] indicate that the incubation period lasts approximately 11 days [ab = approximately 11 days], a value comparable to that reported for the congeneric Foudia madagascariensis and reflecting the rapid embryonic development characteristic of many tropical passerines occupying warm, thermally stable microhabitats. Newly hatched nestlings emerge with a wet weight at birth of roughly 1.6 grams [Wwb = roughly 1.6 grams], placing them among the lighter-bodied neonates of the Ploceinae subfamily. This modest initial mass is consistent with the altricial developmental mode, wherein considerable parental investment in provisioning and brooding is required to support the swift post-hatching growth trajectory necessary to minimize nest predation risk in these structurally exposed reed-bed and sedge nesting sites. The prolonged period of parental attendance is energetically demanding, and female weavers in particular bear a substantial share of the brooding duties while males focus on nest construction and defense.

Adult body size in this species exhibits a moderate degree of sexual dimorphism, a pattern commonly observed among colonial-nesting weavers where competition for nesting territories and female choice play significant roles. Females typically attain an ultimate wet weight of 18 grams [Wwi = 18 grams], whereas males achieve a larger ultimate wet weight of 23.5 grams [Wwi = 23.5 grams], a difference that likely reflects both the energetic demands of nest construction—a task undertaken almost exclusively by males—and the advantages of larger body size in male-male competition for prime nesting sites within the colony. These mass values are intermediate within the genus Ploceus, slotting between the smaller golden weaver (Ploceus subaureus) and the larger village weaver (Ploceus cucullatus). The female mass of 18 grams [Wwi = 18 grams] appears to be a critical threshold for clutch size determination, as body condition at the time of laying strongly influences the number of eggs a female can successfully incubate and provision during the nestling phase. Field measurements taken during the peak breeding season show that individuals in good condition consistently match or exceed these asymptotic weights, while those in poor condition may fall short, resulting in reduced reproductive output for that season.

This relatively modest annual fecundity relative to clutch size is partly constrained by the extended period of post-fledging parental care, which delays the initiation of subsequent nesting attempts.
